name: Uma Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you think privately. What does a usual day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Uma, 43, and I lead the developers of a rental-home repair app at a tech company. I have a master’s degree and I am good at tracing why a tenant’s urgent repair was given a routine ticket. I review overnight cases, fix the rules and check with support staff before release. I use AI now and then to sort long ticket histories after colleagues have tested it, but I read the tenant’s actual report before deciding what is urgent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household picture behind that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Dev, is a paramedic, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My developer pay is high for the job, and we have about eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby. Dev’s shifts are tiring, but we have enough room to take one normal setback without missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau leaves people deciding which repair cannot wait. A quick ticket summary helps. A leaking ceiling still needs the right priority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure about my job and pay. Eight months saved and Dev’s wages give us room for a slow month or a broken appliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking AI ticket summaries against the tenant’s message and call support about urgent errors. I’d continue moving 500 monthly into savings while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask for a named reviewer on every changed emergency-repair rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my income. I would still be annoyed by a repair sent to the wrong queue, but I do not expect staff cuts here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair ticket changed the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ceiling leak was marked routine because the form did not ask whether water was near a light. I changed the question after a support worker read the tenant’s message aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Dev we can keep the children’s holiday plan and still save. I would not treat a strong account as a reason to buy a larger home this year.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people deciding urgent repairs.
I would keep a **named reviewer** on emergency-rule changes.
think: I expect my **lead job and pay** to stay secure.
Our **eight-month savings** and two wages can absorb ordinary setbacks.
do: **Keep** checking ticket summaries against tenant messages and support calls.
**Transfer** 500 monthly into savings while both wages hold.
**Require** a named reviewer for each emergency-repair rule change.
feel: **Calm** about income, while attentive to wrongly queued repairs.
S0.quote: A leaking ceiling still needs the right priority.
fieldNote: Her **tenant-message check** exposed a missing question about water near an electrical light.
High pay, **eight months saved** and many local developer jobs support current financial security.

steps.text: Keep checking repair-ticket summaries against tenant messages
Transfer 500 monthly into savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI write code, sort repairs and answer tenants much faster. I would ask support workers and tenants to test the emergency rules before management cuts review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my lead role might stay, but fewer support workers could mean bad tickets reach me too late. If the developer team shrinks as well, my own hours could be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d compare the approved classifier against twenty past urgent repairs, including the ceiling leak, with support staff. If it catches them all, I’d learn to audit its decisions during paid time. In the first year, if support or developer posts are cut, I’d join our worker council’s meeting to ask for notice and protected review hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, though the reserve buys time. I cannot keep a tenant dry if nobody reads the message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the worker council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the ceiling-leak case to the council and ask who reads reports before a machine labels them routine. I would ask for the test results in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Dev that a reduction in support staff does not automatically mean my pay falls. We would wait for a real staffing notice before changing the children’s plans.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, repair sorting and replies.
I would demand **tenant and support testing** before review time is cut.
think: I worry **fewer support workers** could hide urgent tickets.
I could lose **developer hours** if my team also shrinks.
do: **Test** an approved classifier on twenty old urgent repairs with support staff.
**Learn** to audit its decisions during paid time only if all twenty pass.
**Attend** the worker council if support or developer posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours cuts despite strong savings.
S1.quote: I cannot keep a tenant dry if nobody reads the message.
fieldNote: She sees **support staffing** as part of safety, alongside classifier accuracy and her own hours.
Her **council action** follows actual cuts; paid AI audit learning requires a twenty-case pass.

steps.text: Learn approved repair-classifier audit during paid time if twenty urgent cases pass
Attend worker council if support or developer posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches repair-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so Dev’s paramedic visits may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company could cut most of our developers, including me. Eight months saved buys a search, but a mortgage will keep asking for money if other software jobs shrink too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written severance and keep the proposed home-extension money in cash. I’d list actual local openings, including tenant-support roles, without assuming those survive full AGI. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for real vacancies and eligible income help while protecting Dev’s work transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect my high salary could vanish. Our home extension can wait; the mortgage cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the extension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children their rooms stay as they are while we learn what my job does. I would not call the extension cancelled forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the council help with severance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the worker council to collect severance letters if several teams are cut. We could compare terms and seek paid transition time together.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach repair code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Dev’s **paramedic work** may change later.
think: I expect **major developer cuts** could include me despite my lead role and high pay.
Our **eight-month reserve** cannot guarantee another software job or carry the mortgage forever.
do: **Delay** the home extension and hold its money for mortgage bills.
**Request** written severance; compare letters through council if several teams are cut.
**Apply** for real vacancies and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of a high salary.
S2.quote: Our home extension can wait; the mortgage cannot.
fieldNote: Her **2028 desk-work risk** precedes hands-on robots around 2031 for paramedic work.
The **council effort** requires group cuts; new work and public help depend on vacancies and eligibility.

steps.text: Delay the home extension and reserve its cash for mortgage bills
Compare severance letters through council if several teams are cut
Apply for actual local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to find out what residents need when an urgent repair is missed. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer software jobs, but the extra time lets me test whether I can handle resident complaints, not just code their forms. I cannot assume complaint work stays paid after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d propose a six-week rotation through the tenant-support team, keeping my current pay if management approves. I’d take ownership of six unresolved emergency cases and ask the residents whether the repair was completed. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply only for actual resident-support vacancies that pay enough for our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my coding job, but I can test a real service skill while earning. I would not spend the eight-month reserve on a vague new certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would the six-week rotation produce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring six case outcomes to my manager and ask support to challenge any conclusion I made too quickly. A completed form is not proof a ceiling stopped leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management rejects the rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management refuses a paid rotation, I would keep my current job and volunteer one Saturday with the tenants’ advice group if Dev can cover childcare. I would not call volunteering a replacement income.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test resident service skills.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **fewer software roles** despite warning.
I cannot assume **complaint work** stays paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Complete** a six-week support rotation with current pay protected if approved, resolving six emergency cases.
**Volunteer** one Saturday with the tenants’ advice group if refused and Dev covers childcare.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying support jobs if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code income, with a testable service path.
S3.quote: A completed form is not proof a ceiling stopped leaking.
fieldNote: Her **six-week rotation** produces six checked outcomes rather than a generic certificate.
The **paid rotation** needs approval; volunteering requires refusal and Dev’s childcare, while future jobs need mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Complete approved six-week rotation at current wage and resolve six emergency cases
Volunteer with tenants advice group if rotation refused and Dev covers childcare
Apply after 2031 coding loss for actual resident-support jobs paying mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to make repair records honest and teach newer staff. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay and Dev’s work to hold for now. I still want the company to share decisions with tenants and staff before changing how repairs are reviewed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking urgent-ticket changes against resident reports and save 500 monthly while both wages hold. I’d ask the worker council to hold an annual review with tenants on missed repairs. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search actual local openings before changing the children’s school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long term, though our mortgage feels secure now. I can use the decade to strengthen the people’s voice in the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should attend the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the council to bring three residents with unresolved repair cases, not just managers with charts. I would write down whether each case was actually fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev and I would keep the current house unless an actual offer covers another mortgage and school travel. We would not move children over a forecast.

I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **both wages** to hold in the near term.
I want **tenants and staff** involved before repair-review changes.
do: **Keep** checking urgent tickets with residents and save 500 monthly while wages hold.

Search **actual local openings** after 2036 coding loss before considering any school or home change.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term work, with secure mortgage payments now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my repair-code pay could vanish before Dev’s hands-on work changes. Written severance, paid time to learn resident support and real openings would help. I would also want tenants at the table when the company decides who checks urgent reports.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who walks into a wet kitchen when an app says the leak is routine. A tenant cannot dry the ceiling with a ticket number.

headlineQuote: A tenant cannot dry the ceiling with a ticket number.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, high pay and eight months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** on repair tickets, checking urgent cases against tenant messages and support workers.
Her partner’s **paramedic work** is hands-on; robots follow thinking AI by about three years.
She tests a **paid six-week rotation**, seeks council input and moves only for real mortgage-paying work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her high developer salary before another paid role is established.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid resident-support learning and actual vacancies would help.
